Industry News: Housing groups cheer Senate passage of milestone permitting bill

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.
  • Recent findings suggest that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation.
  • Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.

Recent findings suggest that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation. It is likely one of the last bipartisan measures this Congress will vote on before the 120th Congress is sworn in shortly after the new year.

Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.

BAAJA now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives, which is widely expected to vote on the measure before the new Congress is sworn in on January 3. However, the clock is ticking, as the House is already on Thanksgiving recess. That leaves about a month for the House to either pass the Senate’s version or reconcile any differences between the two chambers.

If the bill doesn’t reach President Trump’s desk by January 3, the process would have to start over with the latest Congress, which would likely change some of its provisions.

Many affordable and multifamily projects that rely on federal funding or assistance face regulatory hurdles that most privately financed housing developments avoid.

These projects include those backed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Examples include housing built using public housing assistance, Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding, USDA housing loans, disaster relief funds and more.

Most notably, these federally backed housing projects must go through National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that don’t apply to most private- sector development projects.

These reviews, critics argue, add an extra regulatory burden that can increase project timelines by a year or more. Critics further contend that NEPA and NHPA, while well-intentioned laws, are often used by NIMBY groups to delay or kill affordable housing development.

In response to these concerns, BAAJA would streamline NEPA reviews for housing development by:.

These changes would strengthen and expand provisions in the HOME Reform Act of 2025, a bill included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that exempted small federal housing projects of 15 units or less from NEPA review.

BAAJA would similarly streamline NHPA reviews and narrow which projects trigger a review, allowing redevelopment projects involving older buildings to move forward more rapidly.

Industry observers note that additionally, the bill would streamline Clean Water Act reviews, in effect speeding up federal wetlands permitting by shortening review timelines and limiting certain EPA interventions and legal challenges. It would also shorten Endangered Species Act consultation timelines and give states a larger role in federal reviews to reduce permitting delays for residential developments on land with protected species or habitats.

Support for BAAJA spans much of the housing industry. Earlier this month, the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, Up for Growth Action and dozens of other housing organizations and homebuilder groups signed a letter urging the Senate to move the permitting reform package forward.

On Friday, National Association of REALTORS Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said in a statement she supports the legislation’s goal of streamlining “permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction and limit housing supply.”.

“These barriers affect everything from starter homes to multifamily rental housing, making it harder to meet the needs of buyers and renters alike,” McGahn noted.

Recent findings suggest that NAHB further argued that BAAJA would reduce land development costs and permitting delays, while also improving multifamily builders’ access to federal housing finance programs. In a statement following the Senate’s vote, NAHB Chairman Bill Owens stated that the bill “will help builders deliver the affordable homes families need.”.

According to recent reports, “By cutting the regulatory costs and delays that drive up the price of construction, BAAJA will expand housing supply, lower costs for buyers and renters and increase access to affordable rental housing. With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay,” Owens stated.

Recent findings suggest that housing is only a fraction of what BAAJA targets. It mainly aims to streamline the development of a wide range of federally backed projects, including:.

As it does for housing, BAAJA would scale back NEPA and other environmental reviews for these federal projects, while also including other measures to shorten permitting and approval timelines.

In the Senate, 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of the bill.

Senators Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were the only Republican Senators to vote against the legislation, largely because they feared it would undermine states’ rights.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, 31 Democrats voted against it. The legislation has drawn significant opposition from environmental groups concerned that its permitting changes could weaken environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel emissions.

Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, for example, argued that the bill “furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands and endangers wildlife.”.

Other critics of BAAJA worry that the bill’s permitting reforms could accelerate the development of more data centers, including on public lands.

Despite the ongoing opposition from environmental groups, BAAJA has bipartisan support in the House. For example, Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who backs the bill’s permitting provisions, countered these concerns by noting that it would also fast-track renewable energy development. He reiterated his support for the bill after it passed the Senate.

“BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us,” Peters said in a statement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking manufacturer, has a fresh CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no prepares to change that.” He remarked he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Recent findings suggest that consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based firm acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and notes it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Sources indicate that zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the manufacturer.

Industry observers note that zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but mentioned Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by newly introduced pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

It has been revealed that zonar has added 1,000 upcoming customers so far this year, a spokesperson noted. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 strategy, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli mentioned.

According to recent reports, zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli remarked Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He stated those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the major players.”.

It has been revealed that consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

Sources indicate that “Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli stated. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

Recent findings suggest that founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • According to recent reports, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

According to recent reports, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

Recent findings suggest that “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont mentioned in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

According to recent reports, “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan remarked in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an key step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

Sources indicate that the solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

According to recent reports, “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s vital to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker mentioned workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

In a recent development, tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really vital component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker remarked. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

#110575. Lock-in effect likely to keep HELOCs, second lien activity up through 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Lock-in effect likely to keep HELOCs, second lien activity up through 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity.
  • According to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan.
  • It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

According to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In a recent development, in October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve Bank of Newly introduced York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

Industry observers note that as a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he said.

Stratis said the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

“Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis said. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

Matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

“Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon said. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a newly introduced roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

Tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his company has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

Hutchens said borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

In a recent development, “Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, mentioned that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

It has been revealed that “[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz stated. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a newly introduced loan, he said. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, said borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

“The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen remarked. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the latest rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

Leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he mentioned, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

Recent findings suggest that for borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz remarked.

Sources indicate that adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, noted home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a newly introduced mortgage.

Industry observers note that “A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson remarked. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions.
  • In a recent development, “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

In a recent development, “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Said another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium:.

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

It has been revealed that “It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he stated during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these newly introduced forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

The financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

In a recent development, the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

“We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he noted during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

In a recent development, infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

“We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

Recent findings suggest that AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

“You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he remarked during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

“What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole organization. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

Alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The tech giant’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

Recent findings suggest that “We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

Sources indicate that keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

“You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he remarked during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:.

Breaking: Bronx real estate broker indicted for allegedly hiding felony convictions on license renewal

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bronx real estate broker Marcia Campbell was arrested and indicted for allegedly failing to disclose felony convictions and pending criminal charges when she applied to renew her Upcoming York real estate broker license, New York Attorney General Letitia James declared Thursday.
  • Recent findings suggest that campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc.
  • Sources indicate that state regulators say that during that June 14, 2024, to June 13, 2026, period, Campbell had in fact pleaded guilty to two felonies in Westchester County and was facing 18 pending charges in Bronx County tied to alleged deed theft and real estate investment scams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bronx real estate broker Marcia Campbell was arrested and indicted for allegedly failing to disclose felony convictions and pending criminal charges when she applied to renew her Upcoming York real estate broker license, New York Attorney General Letitia James declared Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc. in the Bronx, is accused of falsely stating on a June 2026 renewal application that she had not been convicted of a crime and had no criminal charges pending since her previous renewal, according to the announcement from the Office of the Attorney General (OAG).

Sources indicate that state regulators say that during that June 14, 2024, to June 13, 2026, period, Campbell had in fact pleaded guilty to two felonies in Westchester County and was facing 18 pending charges in Bronx County tied to alleged deed theft and real estate investment scams. Once the New York Department of State (DOS) discovered the alleged false statements, her broker license was administratively suspended.

It has been revealed that the case underscores how aggressively Latest York regulators and prosecutors are now scrutinizing license applications and renewals for real estate professionals, particularly in deed theft and fraud matters. For brokers and agents, the case is a reminder that criminal history disclosures on licensing forms are not procedural formalities, but sworn statements that can carry separate felony exposure if falsified.

The upcoming indictment builds on a series of criminal matters involving Campbell in multiple counties.

Industry observers note that in October 2024, Attorney General James and Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark confirmed two separate indictments against Campbell. In the first, she and her co-conspirators — including her husband — were charged in an alleged deed theft scheme involving the childhood home of a Bronx woman. Prosecutors say the group gained the homeowner’s trust, then used fraudulent contracts bearing the homeowner’s forged signature to transfer the property to a shell organization they controlled and to obtain a $493,500 mortgage on the home. Campbell is scheduled to go to trial in that case on Feb. 22, 2027.

The second Bronx indictment accused Campbell of running a series of real estate investment scams. According to prosecutors, she induced clients to send her funds for purported real estate transactions, then kept the money and refused to return most of it. Those alleged scams took more than $250,000 from vulnerable Latest Yorkers, including first-time homebuyers, immigrants and a personal friend, the OAG remarked. A trial date in those cases has not yet been set.

Separate Westchester County prosecutions led to criminal convictions. On Dec. 18, 2025, Campbell pleaded guilty in two cases to Falsifying Business Records in the First Degree and Repeated Failure to File Corporate Taxes, both class E felonies. Authorities said those cases involved an alleged deed theft scheme that targeted three Westchester homes and involved roughly $2 million in fraudulently obtained loans. Campbell was sentenced to time served in those matters.

In a recent development, despite those developments, prosecutors say Campbell submitted a broker license renewal application to DOS in June 2026 covering the period from June 15, 2026, through June 13, 2028. On that application, she allegedly answered “no” to questions asking whether she had been convicted of a crime or had criminal charges pending during the prior licensing period.

Attorney General James alleges Campbell knowingly omitted her December 2025 felony convictions in Westchester County and the 18 Bronx County charges that were already pending at the time she filed the renewal. When DOS identified the discrepancies and referred the matter to law enforcement, the agency suspended Campbell’s license.

Sources indicate that for brokerages, the case highlights the operational risk of failing to monitor the criminal and regulatory status of principal brokers and associated licensees. A suspended or revoked license can jeopardize transactions, commissions and firm reputation, especially in markets where deed theft has drawn heightened scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators.

Sources indicate that upcoming York officials at the state and local level have invested significant resources into deed theft enforcement in recent years, particularly in New York City and surrounding counties where equity-rich but cash-poor homeowners are frequent targets. These schemes often rely on trusted intermediaries, including licensed real estate professionals, to gain access to property records and homeowners.

“New Yorkers depend on real estate brokers to help them make some of the most vital purchases of their lives,” Attorney General James noted in the announcement, adding that Campbell allegedly abused her role “to steal New Yorkers’ homes and savings, then tried to hide her crimes to maintain her license.”.

Recent findings suggest that for compliance officers at brokerages and franchisors, the case signals that state regulators are willing to cross-check licensing records with court and tax data and to bring independent criminal charges based solely on false or incomplete filings. Firms may want to revisit internal policies requiring prompt disclosure of arrests and convictions by licensed personnel and procedures for verifying those disclosures.

Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.
  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software firm, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

Industry observers note that his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health manufacturer Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health looks that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Recent findings suggest that kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their prepares “after we’ve built our product.”.

Sources indicate that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

It has been revealed that searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the proposal.

Sources indicate that why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it states.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Kelman, by his own account, is fresh to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend noted I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman stated the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

According to recent reports, chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software organization he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”.

The Sojourn site states the firm is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

According to recent reports, that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn looks to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

Sources indicate that A new health blueprint typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the organization hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a newly introduced mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He mentioned at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data.
  • XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median.
  • XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana shows the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

It has been revealed that as the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

For comparison, Bitcoin shows an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

Industry observers note that obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a big price move regardless of its direction.

Implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

The chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

For XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

From XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Wimbrow is leaving her role as director of stakeholder relations at the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) after about 20 months to become a vice president at Federal Hall Policy Advisors, she told HousingWire.

Industry observers note that wimbrow, a former FHFA Director Bill Pulte aide, is joining the private sector. POLITICO first reported on her transition. FHFA did not immediately respond to a request for comments.

“I had a great experience at FHFA. It gave me firsthand understanding of the housing finance system and the policy making process, and the importance of the relationship between the government and the agency,” Wimbrow remarked. “My role there was stakeholder relations. So I had a great opportunity to engage with the industry and work with folks in the housing space.”.

During her tenure, Wimbrow noted key discussions with industry participants focused on affordability, credit score modernization, oversight of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and the future of the housing finance system, as well as insurance modernization.

“The industry was very positive with the engagement, and they appreciated the focus of making housing affordable,” she said.

Wimbrow framed the career move as a natural shift from public service to advisory work.

According to recent reports, “I wanted to take what I learned on the agency side, particularly in stakeholder relations and industry engagement, and apply that experience in the private sector,” Wimbrow stated. “It’s a natural step for me to decide on Fed Hall; they lobbied me, and they’re the best in the business.”.

Before joining FHFA, Wimbrow spent three years at the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), most recently as director of Build-PAC, NAHB’s bipartisan political arm focused on federal campaigns.

#110564. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

Recent findings suggest that none could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

Sources indicate that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

Sources indicate that his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be remarked for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

According to recent reports, “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

It has been revealed that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

In a recent development, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she mentioned, but it indicated cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova noted. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Sources indicate that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova stated. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Industry observers note that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney mentioned.

In a recent development, she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

According to recent reports, hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he indicates, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

In a recent development, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

It has been revealed that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

Industry observers note that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer stated. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

In a recent development, shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Recent findings suggest that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein noted.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

According to recent reports, bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova mentioned she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova remarked, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

Latest Update: Howard Hanna sued over $395 real estate transaction fee

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.
  • Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.
  • It has been revealed that bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.

Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.

It has been revealed that bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month.

Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.”.

Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.”.

“It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states.

According to the complaint, the fee was “wedged”  between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner’s title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose.

In the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement, the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing.

Industry observers note that the suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco said she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future.

Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the lawsuit.

The complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee.

Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center, claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year.

  • 18: ULA mentioned Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance.
  • Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA mentioned Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

It has been revealed that that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA mentioned it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA noted. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

In a recent development, ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

Industry observers note that “It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”.

In a recent development, impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Upcoming Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had released 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

According to recent reports, amazon has remarked it prepares to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike Holdings Inc.
  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
  • Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Software buyouts tend to value the acquired organization at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

Sources indicate that crowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a organization’s employees access its business applications.

Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The firm’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity concerns.

It has been revealed that homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Industry observers note that krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

Sources indicate that that opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

It has been revealed that why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The tech giant revealed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it indicates can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this major news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.
