Major crypto exchange Coinbase shared the options-implied seven-day ratios for major cryptocurrencies, highlighting that options traders might be preparing for an unusually large price move for XRP.

In an X post, Coinbase Markets shared the outcome of dividing the options-implied 7-day move by the median 7-day move for XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana.

Options-implied 7d move, divided by each asset's own median 7d move: $XRP 1.94× $BTC 1.69× $ETH 1.56× $SOL 1.46× $XRP is priced furthest above its own history, $SOL the least. Which one is asking for more than its own history delivered? https://t.co/WgWbqjcgwI.

Industry observers note that this suggests how much movement options markets are pricing in relative to each asset's own historical behavior. However, it does not compare their expected dollar or percentage moves directly.

According to recent reports, according to the figures shared by Coinbase, XRP's options-implied seven-day move stands at 1.94 times its own historical median seven-day move. Bitcoin follows at 1.69 times, while Ethereum records 1.56 times and Solana comes in at 1.46 times.

XRP, therefore has the highest relative reading among the four assets, suggesting options traders are pricing in a more pronounced move than the token has typically delivered over a comparable period.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, XRP was down 1.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.98 amid the continued profit-taking in the market. XRP briefly reached $1 on November 18, 2026, but fell afterwards as traders took profits. XRP is down 21.57% so far in November, but its history states more than its current price action does.

In a recent development, XRP’s average November gain is skewed upward by massive outlier rallies—specifically +550% in 2013 and +282% in 2024. Its median November return is about -10%, meaning it has closed lower in most cycles in history. XRP dropped roughly 23.42% in November 2019 and lost 12.18% in November 2025 (opening at around $2.51 and closing at around $2.20).

A weak November doesn’t always mean a weak December: for instance, after falling 9.1% in November 2015, XRP jumped 46.8% in December 2015.

In the near term, XRP’s price recovery will target $1 before moving to the $1.24–$1.26 range. Alternatively, if the price falls further, it is likely to find support at $0.89.

  • “Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” stated Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” stated Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he mentioned.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou noted.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

According to recent reports, for “advanced” users of each organization’s agent tools, it revealed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Industry observers note that partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced latest Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The tech giant is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

In a recent development, the product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

Latest MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella declared that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft claims it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it indicates matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other upcoming business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Firm consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff revealed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

It has been revealed that the cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A upcoming Agent 365 Business Analytics feature demonstrates business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

Recent findings suggest that in another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#110539. Industry News: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions

Industry News: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S.
  • In a recent development, but while this long-overdue action can help U.S.
  • The Trump administration wants the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole.

In a recent development, but while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there’s still a paradox at the heart of Washington’s AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction.

The Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president’s vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.

But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn’t just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too.

In a recent development, today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global consumers.

Chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones.

The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration’s dreams of AI dominance is that success at one layer of the stack is undermining its goals at another.

When people hear that Chinese models are gaining customers, they generally assume that those models are running on Chinese chips. While that’s increasingly the case within China, the truth is that China cannot produce enough advanced AI chips to satisfy its own companies, let alone meet overseas demand.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, America’s grip on AI infrastructure is formidable. U.S. companies—Nvidia, Google, AMD, and Amazon—design nearly all deployed data-center AI chips. In cloud services, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google together control more than half of the market, with a growing cohort of U.S. “neoclouds” further extending that lead.

Yet the same infrastructure that secures America’s advantage in chips and cloud services gives Chinese AI models a platform to spread. Nvidia itself provides resources to help companies deploy open models—including several Chinese models—on its hardware. U.S.-based model inference providers such as Together AI, Baseten, and Fireworks serve Chinese models to people on infrastructure powered by U.S. chips. For example, DeepSeek’s latest model is being offered by at least 16 inference providers headquartered outside China, including Amazon Bedrock.

Sources indicate that when U.S. infrastructure is used to serve Chinese LLMs, it accelerates those models’ global adoption, which in turn benefits China’s soft power and generates revenue for its AI labs. Beijing’s stated ambition is to be the leading provider of transformative AI capabilities, especially in the Global South. Wider adoption of Chinese LLMs advances that objective.

Chinese LLM deployments also generate direct revenue for Chinese model developers. For example, Moonshot AI requires companies that serve its successful Kimi K3 model and exceed $20 million in annual sales to negotiate a revenue-sharing license; Moonshot has reportedly asked Microsoft, Amazon, and Google for 30% of their Kimi K3 revenue.

Today, who benefits from U.S. computing infrastructure depends on whether it serves proprietary or open-weight models. On one side are proprietary LLMs such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s GPT. Infrastructure serving proprietary models almost exclusively benefits American developers, because they make the best ones. On the other side are open-weight LLMs, which companies can customize for specialized tasks and run locally. Infrastructure serving open-weight LLMs benefits Chinese developers: users tend to choose the best available models, and in the open-weight market, those are Chinese.

According to recent reports, the Trump administration, however, should not go so far as to ban U.S. cloud providers from allowing non-Chinese companies to serve Chinese LLMs. Doing so would incur too high a cost—unjustifiably hindering companies in the United States and allied countries seeking to adopt AI—while failing to deliver sufficient national security benefits. It could also invite Chinese retaliation.

Instead, the United States should compete. Some U.S. companies like Meta and Thinking Machines are already developing open-weight models. If they become more cost-efficient than their Chinese competitors, more U.S. computing infrastructure would serve U.S. models. That shift could limit both the revenue Chinese developers earn from overseas deployments and the soft power China gains from its models’ global reach.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration is therefore correct to encourage the development of competitive U.S. open-weight models. It should identify government uses well-suited to open-weight models and direct federal procurement toward American open-weight models for those uses. Finally, as stronger AI regulation becomes necessary, the administration should design those rules carefully to avoid stifling U.S. open-weight model development.

Sources indicate that washington can’t assume that exporting U.S. infrastructure will automatically lead to the export of U.S. models. If it wants to succeed on both fronts, it needs a deliberate strategy for open-weight models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

On Nov. 18, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms. The listing covers the web interface of the Hyperliquid trading terminal at app.hyperliquid.xyz/trade. The HYPE token dropped to around $65.50 on the evening of Nov. 18, and it recovered to $68.79 by midday Nov. 19, according to TradingView data.

In a recent development, according to the entry, the company claims to provide digital asset trading services on the website, and it has no address on record. Hyperliquid is not licensed by the SFC, and it is suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or actively promoting its services to the public, the regulator noted.

In an accompanying warning, the SFC reminded investors that such platforms often lure customers with "incredible investment opportunities." The SFC also reminded investors that clients of unlicensed platforms have no legal protection if a platform is hacked or misappropriates their assets.

In a recent development, on the same day, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority with seven recommendations on the country's fresh crypto rules. "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity," the group wrote.

On Nov. 16, two days before the SFC added Hyperliquid to the list, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan spoke at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. "Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter," Chan remarked.

According to Chan, the bill will cover crypto dealers, custodians, advisers and asset managers. "Decentralisation does not mean less accountability," he said.

In April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority licensed HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial as the first stablecoin issuers in the city, out of 36 applicants in the first round.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 5:15 pm.

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in latest funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other projects.

Founded last year, the manufacturer says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team noted it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more vital than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason noted in a statement.

The firm combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

Recent findings suggest that the latest funding brings Aarden’s total investments to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The firm has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason noted he released the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, noted the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson mentioned on LinkedIn.

#110535. Tech Report: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns

Tech Report: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.
  • China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S.
  • That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni noted in a note earlier this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni noted in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his proposal to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.

Industry observers note that real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.

Industry observers note that “To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note mentioned. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”.

Retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.

Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.

To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.

“Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.

According to recent reports, “China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”.

Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.

It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for company buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.

According to recent reports, but the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a fresh risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.

“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.

Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it.
  • In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s very notable to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:48 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

In a recent development, A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

According to recent reports, “It’s very notable to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller stated. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”.

Industry observers note that koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.).

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

Industry observers note that “The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”.

It has been revealed that that pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller remarked. “We have to look for the data.”.

Sources indicate that efficiency is part of the equation, too. The latest system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

In a recent development, “We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller stated. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”.

The 86 trillion threshold has been a sinister cloud over Shiba Inu. For now, it might take a step back, thanks to decreasing selling pressure on the market according to CryptoQuant. The token's technical state isn't great, unfortunately, as it's struggling to find fuel for a recovery.

Shiba Inu printed only 67 billion in exchange inflows, which is a 67% decrease from the local peak of 250 billion. The decreasing exchange inflows are a signal of decreasing selling pressure, even though the available supply on exchanges is still enormous.

Recent findings suggest that according to CryptoQuant, exchange reserves currently sit at around 85.74 trillion SHIB, worth approximately $332.68 million. They're still up by 0.04% over the last 24 hours.

The real question here is obviously the recovery potential: a decrease in selling pressure quite often precedes recoveries, but it's important to keep in mind that SHIB has barely found the fuel to decelerate the bearish trend, let alone retrace in price.

SHIB's price is stagnant at around $0.000004 and is unlikely to find a footing for a move up anytime soon.

The ascending trendline that held the price since July was broken in mid-October, which opened the way toward more losses. Shiba Inu mostly followed the general downtrend but tumbled promptly in one daily candle in the middle of November, and it has been moving sideways since then. Volume on the day of the drop was lower than the spikes in August and September.

It has been revealed that all five moving averages on the chart stay above the price, and the closest one sits around $0.0000044. The June and July lows near $0.0000041 are already behind us, so there's no clear support on the chart below, unfortunately.

The RSI dropped into the oversold zone on the day of that drop and hasn't climbed far from it since. Momentum remains bearish: SHIB's RSI is at 25, a clear oversold signal, even though there's barely any buying volume on the market.

#110531. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (646 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.
  • Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.
  • The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”.

Industry observers note that the change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

According to recent reports, muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

Industry observers note that for Muse people, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas noted any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

It has been revealed that what’s newly introduced is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Recent findings suggest that meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

It has been revealed that amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has mentioned Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy remarked outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 joined the Nasdaq in correction territory as AI stocks plunged further, but 2026 is also winding down, and Wall Street is already putting out predictions for 2027.

In a recent development, analysts see solid gains ahead, with the U.S. economy expected to continue chugging along on the back of massive hyperscaler spending and resilient consumers. Some also welcomed the recent decline for taking froth off markets that might otherwise start looking overheated.

Even this week’s selloff, which marked the worst weekly loss since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, was largely dismissed as a move driven more by emotion than fundamentals.

“This does not mean stampedes are uninformative or palpitations never presage heart attacks, but today’s panic does not feel like an AI bust,” Viktor Shvets, head of global desk strategy at Macquarie Capital, said in a note Friday.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager and partner at Founder ETFs, quipped that the market is “selling first and asking questions later.” And Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group, predicted investors will “return to rationality” and look instead to consumption-boosting GDP.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Morgan Stanley chief U.S. equity strategist Michael Wilson said earlier this week that the S&P 500 would finish 2027 at 8,700, representing a 26% jump from current levels and a 15% rally when he made the call.

“We see the mid-cycle transition now ending with a more stable mid-cycle backdrop evolving in 2027,” he wrote.

Goldman Sachs also sees the broad market index soaring to 8,700 next year, “albeit with higher volatility than in recent years.”.

Recent findings suggest that peter Oppenheimer, the bank’s chief global equity strategist, noted that while corporate earnings growth will slow, inflation, bond yields, and oil prices will also moderate. “We expect the equity bull market to continue.”.

Elsewhere, estimates were less bullish but still upbeat. UBS Global Wealth Management put the S&P 500 at 8,200 next year, implying 19% upside from Friday’s close.

Although it sees more earnings gains in 2027, Wall Street is focusing on whether the investment cycle can support profits into 2028, UBS explained.

According to recent reports, “Cannibalization, financing, and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high,” it added. “The market is therefore more sensitive to earnings disappointment or a further rise in discount rates.”.

Wells Fargo’s S&P 500 outlook in 2027 is also for 8,200, which assumes slower profit growth as well.

But then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels.

Industry observers note that he brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive.

“A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued.

Slower prices could prevent additional rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, which has grown more hawkish as policymakers become impatient with inflation exceeding their 2% target for over five years.

Although Wall Street sees more tightening in the coming months, some analysts also anticipate rate cuts later in 2027 as inflation cools. But that assumes the Iran war will be over some time next year.

For now, Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at Modera Wealth Management, described the market slide as a “garden variety correction,” with stock leadership rotating from tech to industrials and financials.

Industry observers note that “The pullback in stocks sets the market up nicely for 2027, which we believe will be a high-single-digit year,” he added. “Multiples are shrinking, and total returns are a function of earnings growth, which so far looks robust for 2027.”.

#110529. Tech Report: Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1178 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • According to recent reports, for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • A tech giant can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A tech giant can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

Industry observers note that the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Recent findings suggest that institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an key regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

Industry observers note that as an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health intends and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

According to recent reports, early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Recent findings suggest that has the founder or company addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

In a recent development, these challenges make the earliest stages of organization formation particularly crucial. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

In a recent development, at Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the tech giant is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

In a recent development, AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

In a recent development, the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Moving swiftly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a organization needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

It has been revealed that companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

In a recent development, the numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data highlights. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

Sources indicate that the biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based tech giant is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

Recent findings suggest that customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, Latest York-based ElevenLabs revealed a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

Recent findings suggest that voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean manufacturer behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram confirmed plans to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”.

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am.

Sources indicate that jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the firm for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos remarked. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”.

Nvidia’s board says it has no prepares to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

Jones mentioned the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place swiftly but won’t rush the pick.

It has been revealed that huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He noted he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Industry observers note that nvidia revealed Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

Recent findings suggest that he stated he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”.

It has been revealed that huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the firm.

Recent findings suggest that the Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also mentioned Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Sources indicate that business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she mentioned customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”.

In a recent development, in case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”.

Recent findings suggest that binance will delist five crypto spot trading pairs within the next 24 hours on Nov. 20, 2026, following a review.

To protect its people and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

Four of the five affected pairs are related to the Turkish lira (TRY), while the last one is HBAR/BNB. The decision affects trading between these specific assets and does not mean the cryptocurrencies themselves are being completely delisted from Binance.

The exchange clarified that people will still be able to trade the affected tokens through other available spot trading pairs on its platform.

In a recent development, binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. People are strongly advised to update and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

Sources indicate that in related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

It has been revealed that affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in owners’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

It has been revealed that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any organization planning to problem under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

Industry observers note that the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

According to recent reports, the Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Sources indicate that under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

It has been revealed that the difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

  • “I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That firm was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she stated, well there is this firm called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”.

Industry observers note that “Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I stated, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”.

“And I noted, I’ll take the cigarette job.”.

It has been revealed that patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and swiftly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

“They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”.

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and noted this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

Sources indicate that “I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”.

The United Nations Environment Programme's Global Waste Management Outlook 2024 projects that annual global MSW generation will reach 3.8 billion metric tons by 2050. Mixed collection and complex waste composition make effective sorting an important step in recovering materials for further use.

DataBeyond combines AI hyperspectral optical sorting with robotic picking to recover recyclable materials from mixed waste. Optical sorters process high-volume material streams, while robots identify and pick individual recyclable items from complex mixtures. The combination helps operators expand material recovery and reduce reliance on manual sorting in demanding environments.

In MSW applications, the firm's systems recover target plastics, including polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) films, while separating materials that are incompatible with the intended recycling process. Suitable recovered fractions can then be washed and processed into feedstock for manufacturing, helping reduce the amount of waste sent for final disposal.

Recent findings suggest that for plastics recycling, DataBeyond offers AI hyperspectral optical sorters that distinguish materials by composition, including plastics with similar appearances. Applications cover mixed rigid plastics, PET bottles and PET flakes. By separating incompatible polymers and improving material consistency, the systems help recyclers prepare feedstock for downstream manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that in textile recycling, the FASTSORT-TEXTILE-AI-SPEC system from DataBeyond sorts used garments by fiber composition, including cotton and polyester content. Further sorting of shredded textiles can remove fragments containing buttons, zippers and other unwanted components. These processes help prepare textile feedstock for suitable textile-to-textile recycling routes. The Fastsort-Textile optical fabric sorter received a Special Mention in TIME's Best Inventions of 2025.

Through these efforts, DataBeyond aims to connect recovery businesses with manufacturers seeking recycled feedstock, helping more recovered materials meet production requirements and return to supply chains.

In a recent development, founded in 2018, Hangzhou DataBeyond Technology Co., Ltd. develops intelligent waste-sorting equipment and integrated solutions using AI, optical sensing and robotics. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he remarked, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a organization.

According to recent reports, we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your intends for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

In a recent development, revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in fresh customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

It has been revealed that before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

It has been revealed that so figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a substantial deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

It has been revealed that look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a upcoming calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

According to recent reports, for the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to overhaul the whole manufacturer all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Sources indicate that jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a firm.

It has been revealed that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.
