📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You noted spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

Recent findings suggest that “The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

Industry observers note that “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom remarked, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We revealed up and remarked, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

It has been revealed that cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

Industry observers note that “The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she noted. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

In a recent development, fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith remarked.

Industry observers note that the region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn stated, should be judged by the communities themselves.

According to recent reports, “And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he mentioned. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder noted he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The Latest York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

According to recent reports, “By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

According to recent reports, “We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the massive moves: landing a major client, launching a upcoming service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Recent findings suggest that ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

Industry observers note that none of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

One of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly big difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine.

The more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it.

And it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target.

Recent findings suggest that over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk.

Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions.

According to recent reports, walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses.

In a recent development, and it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference.

Now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself.

Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business.

Sources indicate that taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing fresh ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch.

Sources indicate that I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in fresh ones.

Over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep.

Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find new projects.

One small habit that has made a significant difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them.

Sources indicate that I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices.

I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time.

It has been revealed that over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%.

Recent findings suggest that I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more vital today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching consumers’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers.

According to recent reports, business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend.

One habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage.

In a recent development, I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return.

Even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships.

I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting.

These relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals vital or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch.

Business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published.

According to recent reports, if you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.

Taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel important in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a newly introduced service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Recent findings suggest that ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. It has been revealed that none of these were clever strategies or massive investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

According to recent reports, the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

A Monero token crashed 99% on Friday after 5.2 million XMR1 tokens moved from a wallet tied to its creator, triggering a massive sell-off on Hyperliquid. The token, issued through crypto swap service Wagyu, plunged from around $494 to below $1 in 35 minutes. The wallet receiving the tokens sold enough to generate $13.22 million in USDC before converting the proceeds into 7,467 ETH.

Industry observers note that wagyu’s wallet security and the backing behind its wrapped Monero product are being questioned. And the sell-off also sent shockwaves through the Monero market, although native XMR remained a separate asset from the collapsing XMR1 market.

Sources indicate that the incident began this morning when the account responsible for deploying XMR1 transferred tokens to a newly created wallet. Blockchain intelligence firm Bitquery identified three separate transfers between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. Two transactions moved 100,000 XMR1 each, followed by a much larger transfer of 5 million tokens.

The receiving wallet had been created that morning. It began selling shortly after receiving the tokens, overwhelming buyers on Hyperliquid’s order book. XMR1 had traded near $500 throughout the previous week. Its price then collapsed to about $1 within roughly 35 minutes, leaving holders with almost nothing.

Bitquery traced 363,804 tokens sold for $13.5 million. The remaining 4.83 million tokens stayed in the receiving wallet during its investigation. The sell-off also exposed how concentrated XMR1’s supply had been. Before the transfers, its deployer account still controlled 93% of the token’s supply.

Sources indicate that hyperliquid transfers require signatures from the account’s own key, rather than an ordinary trading API wallet. This means whoever authorized the transfers likely had access to the deployer’s main key. Whether someone stole that access or used it legitimately remains unknown.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

Industry observers note that the damage extended beyond traders watching XMR1 collapse on their screens. Bitquery matched the seller’s transactions against 388 accounts that purchased the dumped tokens. One buyer alone paid $3.56 million, while 27 large buyers accounted for 77% of the total proceeds.

Industry observers note that the wallet did not leave the money sitting in USDC. It began moving funds through Hyperliquid’s bridge into Arbitrum shortly after selling.

XMR1 hack: 388 Hyperliquid buyers paid $13.50 million for a token that fell 99.8%https://t.co/k5ggHcH6Al.

In a recent development, on Arbitrum, the wallet exchanged $13.22 million in USDC for 7,467 ETH through CoW Protocol. It then routed much of the Ethereum through Socket, Mayan, and Stargate. 6,810 ETH then arrived on Ethereum after those bridge transactions. Approximately 4,836 ETH landed in a newly created wallet that had not sent any funds onward.

The investigation also identified 7,348 ETH across three wallets during its tracking window. That left a substantial amount of the proceeds sitting outside the original trading account.

The incident has put Wagyu’s bridge infrastructure under scrutiny. XMR1 represents Monero on Hyperliquid and is issued through Wagyu’s bridging service. Owners can move native XMR into the service and receive XMR1 for trading. They can also reverse the process to recover their Monero.

Sources indicate that native XMR did not suffer the same collapse. Monero continued trading around $470–$482, while XMR1 lost virtually all its market value.

Holders now face a difficult question: Can they still exchange their remaining XMR1 for native Monero?

The incident also comes weeks after Wagyu disclosed a separate data leak on October 28. Researchers identified exposed records potentially linking crypto deposits, Monero receiving addresses, and customer IP addresses.

Industry observers note that wagyu previously stated customer funds remained unaffected by that incident. No established connection links the October leak to Friday’s wallet transfers.

Recent findings suggest that the latest investigation also uncovered another potential concern. The same deployer account controls 99.97% of ZEC1, a separate token representing Zcash on Hyperliquid.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the firm prepares to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

In a recent development, panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

Industry observers note that while the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky remarked. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Industry observers note that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

In a recent development, berdichevsky remarked Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In a recent development, in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The firm must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

Industry observers note that the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The tech giant has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round confirmed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

In a recent development, seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

In a recent development, group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced intends for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky mentioned.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our tech giant’s history,” he remarked.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app indicates the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

Sources indicate that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Recent findings suggest that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

Industry observers note that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

According to recent reports, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

In a recent development, the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

Recent findings suggest that the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Industry News: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too substantial to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too substantial to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

According to recent reports, “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” stated Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”.

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy remarked there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Recent findings suggest that annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he stated. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the firm in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” stated Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise looks.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy mentioned. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Industry observers note that duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The fresh products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Industry observers note that plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The latest products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he remarked.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy mentioned. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Sources indicate that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

Sources indicate that the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Sources indicate that duffy noted Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the manufacturer, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

It has been revealed that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy remarked Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building upcoming products.

It has been revealed that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the firm, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that I run a global business called Brand of a Leader, which supports founders and executives in more than 12 countries by helping them build their visibility. When I first launched my business six years ago, all I had was a LinkedIn profile — no website and, naturally, no digital footprint of any kind yet.

And so our first few clients came through my network. By being active on LinkedIn and consistently sharing my perspective, I would stay top of mind with people who already knew me. When they needed support, or when someone in their own network did, I was the one who came to mind and was hired or recommended.

It has been revealed that today, I continue to use LinkedIn actively to generate clients, develop relationships and stay connected with my network. I’ve been on the platform for over 20 years, and throughout the years, I’ve heard people constantly complain about one thing: the algorithm. I always chuckle because the discourse is consistently the same, yet it’s presented as something new. Through all of my work and my extensive work supporting founders across the globe with their LinkedIn, I’ve seen how much people overindex on what to post, when to post and how to post, while overlooking something else that is likely even more crucial!

In a recent development, here are the three mistakes I see founders make all the time. And I promise that if you fix those, you will see better results from this platform.

Industry observers note that obsession over what, when and how to post is real. Short posts or long posts? Daily or weekly? With a photo? Video? No media? What should I even write about? Those are undoubtedly crucial questions, yet there’s another one: What happens when someone reads your post, does become interested in learning more about you and then clicks on your profile?

My experience shows me that most founders don’t pay much attention to what’s actually on their profile. I know this because I constantly audit LinkedIn pages as part of the service that we provide at Brand of a Leader.

Too often, when I visit a LinkedIn profile, I find a bland banner or none whatsoever, and a short “About” section written in the third person. Whatever interest the person’s post may have piqued is rapidly lost when visiting their uninspiring profile.

Personally, I treat my profile as a landing page. And we do the same for our clients. For entrepreneurs, myself included, a well-designed LinkedIn page can be a practical alternative to a personal website when used thoughtfully.

Visit your profile, looking at it through the eyes of a potential client, and see what impression it would leave on them after spending a minute or two scrolling through it.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things we consistently convince our clients not to do is include calls to action in their posts. Salesy or overly promotional messages on founders’ profiles don’t make a great impression.

Sources indicate that as a reader, I find that repeated prompts to book a call can make otherwise thoughtful writing feel overly promotional. I prefer to keep my content, and my clients’ content, conversational, expertise-building or humanizing. Yet, I do understand the importance of giving interested readers a clearly visible way to take the next step.

It has been revealed that instead of salesy calls to action in posts, I leverage the custom call-to-action button included with LinkedIn Premium Business. You can have it say anything that’s most relevant to you and your goals (for example, “Visit my website” or “Book a call”). This link will appear in your profile, just under your name and above the post that you write. That feels more elegant to me.

One of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is treating LinkedIn as a broadcasting platform and not a social media platform. This is not only the quickest way to reduce the overall engagement of your content on LinkedIn, but it’s also not great for your positioning overall. When you only post and never engage, it positions you as a taker, not a giver, and also discourages people from further engaging with you.

At a minimum, you need to reply to people who took the time to comment on your posts. No, not only a “like” — an actual thoughtful reply. They have taken time to respond to something you shared. Read their contribution and respond to the substance of it.

Sources indicate that and then ideally, extend that attention to other people’s content. Comment to share a relevant experience or ask a thoughtful question. If someone describes a challenge you have faced, explain what you learned. But don’t use AI. Generic, bland comments negatively impact your brand equity. Take 30 minutes to leave some authentic comments a couple of times weekly, and that consistency will compound over time.

Before publishing your next post, think about what interested readers will see on your profile if they click on it. Give them enough context to understand your expertise, an easy way to contact you and your attention when they engage in conversation with you.

Before you hit publish again, take a look at LinkedIn’s latest Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make sure your profile is ready when interested readers click through.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before Raj Shamani sat in a room with some of the most influential people in the world, he had to figure out how to stop his bedroom from echoing.

Sources indicate that the aspiring podcaster didn’t have a studio or connections to the successful people he wanted to meet. So, he sat in his bedroom in Indore, India, pulled a blanket over his head, and pressed record—figuring the best way to learn how to build a successful business was to ask the people who already had.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t have capital. I didn’t have connections. I didn’t have the access to people who could teach me,” Shamani told Fortune. “Initially it was selfish, I just wanted to learn.”.

It has been revealed that shamani got his first taste of entrepreneurship at 16, when he began helping with his father’s chemical-trading business after a health scare. He learned to make dishwashing liquid by watching YouTube videos, then started selling it door to door in his hometown of Indore. He eventually developed his own cleaning product, Jadugar Drop, before turning to public speaking and content creation.

Recent findings suggest that he didn’t get podcasting right on his first try. Or his second. One show lasted only a few days; another fizzled out because he couldn’t find guests. But none of that seemed to shake his confidence. In December 2020, he introduced Figuring Out.

Shamani called himself “extremely delusional,” believing he can succeed despite knowing he’s not the most talented person in the room, doesn’t have the best connections, and doesn’t have the deepest pockets.

According to recent reports, “I don’t have all of this,” he noted. “But what I have is I can outwork everybody, and that selfawareness helped me.”.

In a recent development, his team now records about 200 episodes annually, but publishes only around 150, scrapping the dozens that don’t make the cut. While other podcasters compete to land the biggest names, Shamani claims his team approaches each conversation like a product, built around a problem its audience wants solved.

“We weren’t competing for the biggest guest, we were competing for the most valuable question,” he said.

In a recent development, another finding was less flattering for the man behind the microphone and camera. When Shamani spoke more than his guest during the first seven minutes, viewers were more likely to leave. So he began opening with a short question and letting his guests take over.

According to recent reports, the firm has also turned to AI to help take its podcast beyond India. Using multilingual audio tracks and dubbing tools, the team distributes conversations in Hindi, English, and Spanish, then creates clips tailored to different countries, regions, and even American states. Shamani mentioned the share of his audience outside India has soared from roughly 3% to 22%, with a surprise jump in Australia.

That same technology helps decide what gets recorded in the first place. Before Shamani sits down with a guest, his team uses AI to study audience interests, select topics, vet potential interviewees, and prepare research briefs running 30 to 40 pages, along with roughly 100 suggested questions.

But once the camera starts rolling, Shamani leaves the calculations behind. “I need to be the most human version of myself,” he noted. “After and before, it’s all science.”.

Recent findings suggest that some of Shamani’s biggest business decisions have come from the people sitting across from him. After interviewing the founders of Indian consumer goods brand Mamaearth about the importance of “founder energy,” he had his first three employees live with him for a year. Those early hires now lead major departments at his company.

Olympic swimmer Michael Phelps, meanwhile, taught him to visualize success even when things go wrong, a practice Shamani now uses before interviews.

It has been revealed that figuring Out Media has since expanded into educational courses, investments, and a social media distribution business called Relevance Media. A consumer goods division is also in the works, part of Shamani’s ambition to build a manufacturer that can survive long after he stops appearing in front of the camera.

“There’s a creator and a organization around him, and then there’s a company which happens to have a creator,” he noted. “I think I’m building the latter one.”.

Although XRP is at risk of losing its top-four position in the global cryptocurrency market, the asset still ranks among the three largest crypto assets in Japan.

In a recent post shared by the renowned Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth, the company highlighted XRP’s growing performance in the Japan crypto market.

Earlier today, Evernorth shared monthly data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto Assets Exchange Association (JVCEA) revealing that XRP recorded about ¥132.8 billion in spot trading volume in September 2026.

While this accounted for about 15% of Japan's total crypto spot trading volume during the month, XRP emerged as the third most-traded cryptocurrency in Japan after Bitcoin and Ethereum.

This highlights that XRP has outperformed other major altcoins that are currently trading in the Japan crypto market, hitting about $880 million in trading volume.

While further data highlighted Solana and Dogecoin ranking next to XRP on the list as the fourth- and fifth-largest cryptocurrencies in Japan, respectively, the data also showed a wide gap from XRP’s ¥132.8 billion spot volume.

This means that XRP is significantly ahead of Solana and Dogecoin in the Japan crypto trading market, as Solana recorded only about ¥19.47 billion in trading volume during the same month.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, saw less participation, as it recorded only ¥11.27 billion in spot volume during the same period.

With XRP sitting in the third spot, the asset has become one of the most actively traded cryptocurrencies in Japan despite its persistent price volatility.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, daily pool data indicates Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

According to recent reports, across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

Industry observers note that NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

Recent findings suggest that the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

Industry observers note that ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest revision on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

According to recent reports, small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

Industry observers note that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

Sources indicate that the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations.
  • The limitations have been understood for some time.
  • For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business?

The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it revealed how much weight public markets now place on a single private tech giant’s numbers.

For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing.

Sources indicate that ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting.

Industry observers note that the first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month.

Industry observers note that what gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts.

It has been revealed that companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable.

Sources indicate that take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter.

These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that.

If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size.

Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises.

Sources indicate that retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked.

ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon.

What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could.

Sources indicate that kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global, based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders.

Bitcoin price has fallen below $62,000 for the first time since early July, extending a brutal November selloff as institutional investors pull billions from the market. BTC touched $61,270 just now, before recovering slightly to trade around $61,700.

Industry observers note that bitcoin price has now lost more than 10% over seven days, with selling pressure spreading across equities, precious metals and other risk assets. Yesterday’s $582.3 million outflow from US spot Bitcoin ETFs added another blow, bringing November withdrawals close to $3.5 billion.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest single-day outflow since launching. The same session saw $727 million in crypto liquidations, with bullish traders absorbing most of the damage.

Institutional demand is weakening, leveraged buyers are being forced out, and the Federal Reserve’s increasingly hawkish outlook is making speculative assets less attractive.

Bitcoin is now approaching $60,000, a level that could determine if the correction finds a floor or develops into something uglier.

The ETF withdrawals are arguably the biggest concern for Bitcoin holders right now. Spot Bitcoin ETFs became an vital source of institutional demand after launching in January 2024. Their buying helped absorb available supply and gave traditional investors a regulated route into the market.

That demand is now moving in the opposite direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost more than $1.1 billion this week alone. November’s cumulative withdrawals have approached $3.5 billion.

Industry observers note that the pressure extends beyond ETFs. Rising Treasury yields and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase in December have encouraged investors to reduce exposure to assets that offer no regular income.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, derivatives traders are taking heavy losses. CoinGlass data showed more than $700 million in liquidations across crypto markets over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for 86% of the total.

Bitcoin itself recorded nearly $202 million in liquidations, with bullish traders suffering the majority of forced closures.

In a recent development, this creates a difficult environment for buyers. Falling prices trigger liquidations, which create additional selling pressure and push prices lower. The reduction in open interest also suggests excessive leverage is being flushed from the market.

The immediate battle is around $60,000. Bitcoin needs to reclaim $62,000 and establish support above it before bulls can confidently argue that the latest breakdown was temporary.

There are three possible scenarios:.

Scenario 1: Bitcoin loses $60K and heads toward $58K or $53K.

Industry observers note that this is the bearish outcome. A decisive break below $60,000 could trigger another wave of stop-loss orders and leveraged liquidations.

The next downside area sits around $58,000, while more aggressive technical projections point toward $53,700.

In a recent development, the daily chart offers little encouragement for bulls. Bitcoin trades below its major moving averages, while bearish momentum continues to dominate. A sustained recovery in ETF flows would become increasingly vital to prevent further deterioration.

Scenario 2: Bitcoin stabilizes between $60K and $62K.

This would give buyers time to absorb available supply without immediately reversing the entire November decline.

The liquidation wave has already removed considerable leverage from the market. If ETF withdrawals begin slowing, Bitcoin could establish a trading range before attempting another recovery.

It has been revealed that but sideways trading alone would not confirm a bottom. Buyers need to demonstrate that they can defend support through multiple sessions.

Scenario 3: Bitcoin reclaims $62K and launches a relief rally.

A recovery above $62,000 would provide the first meaningful sign that sellers are losing control. A move toward $65,000 would then become possible, followed by resistance around $68,000.

Consistent ETF inflows, improving market sentiment, and a weaker dollar would strengthen this scenario. Without those developments, any rebound risks becoming another opportunity for sellers to exit.

In a recent development, for existing holders, the decision depends heavily on their entry price, investment horizon, and exposure. Long-term holders who bought substantially below current prices have more room to withstand volatility. Selling simply because Bitcoin crossed a psychological threshold risks locking in profits or losses without knowing whether the broader investment thesis has changed.

However, investors holding leveraged positions face a different problem. Falling prices can trigger forced liquidations regardless of their long-term convictions. Reducing leverage and protecting available capital should take priority over waiting for a rebound.

For buyers, the temptation to buy the dip is understandable. Bitcoin is considerably cheaper than it was just weeks ago, but cheaper does not automatically mean undervalued.

Buying in stages rather than committing an entire allocation around $61,000 offers more flexibility if the market tests $58,000 or even $53,700.

In a recent development, bitcoin price remains vulnerable to another leg down. The $60,000 level is no longer just a psychological milestone. It is where the next major battle between buyers and sellers will be fought.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year.
  • According to recent reports, AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

According to recent reports, AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

You’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription company is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

Most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

“Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

In a recent development, let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as rapidly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

Most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

The holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

Finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

According to recent reports, what exactly will your business or tech giant gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

It’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

Industry observers note that people with a personal relationship with an employee or manufacturer respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

Personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

If Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

Sources indicate that I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Sources indicate that last month, I received a statement from the company that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the newly introduced owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

Industry observers note that the next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

The holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both newly introduced and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

But why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

Many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

It has been revealed that this also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

It has been revealed that don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

In a recent development, here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

Industry observers note that as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

It has been revealed that AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

At the 2026 Breakpoint event, Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza, gave a walkthrough of Solana’s wins this year, while sharing what is in store for 2027.

According to Watt, 2026 was a major year for Solana as it migrated its consensus to Alpenglow, slashed the block times in half from 400 ms to 200 ms while doubling capacity.

The Alpenglow upgrade went live on mainnet on October 21, 2026, cutting transaction finality from about 12.8 seconds down to roughly 150 milliseconds. It replaced TowerBFT with Votor, a faster path to reaching agreement.

After Alpenglow, @bw_solana laid out @anza_xyz roadmap for Solana in 2027 Performance: network compute capacity doubles, transactions cut 80% CU units for token accounts Expressivity: vector processing for models running fully onchain, 64 → 96 accounts per transaction, read account data instead of copying it so less data moves per transaction Market Structure: Alpenglow. Next with faster block distribution and Constellation for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators Resilience: simpler protocol with fewer special cases, safer to change https://t.co/EpvDdSyjln.

Recent findings suggest that solana recently transitioned to 1.0, marking the network’s graduation from “mainnet beta” to “mainnet” and retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch. Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience.

Sources indicate that according to Watt, Solana is eyeing significant improvements in 2027 across four categories. First is Resilience, which involves simplifying the protocol, reducing special cases, and making it safer to change.

“So, we're going to go ahead and simplify the protocol, replacing legacy abstractions and interfaces, pushing more of the execution on chain, and modernizing some of the wire formats. And all of this, you know, enhances resiliency, but it also allows us to move quicker and be more agile and deploy things and evolve the protocol more quickly,” Watt stated.

Second is Market Structure, which centers on Alpenglow, which aims for faster block distribution, and Constellation, which aims for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators.

“Several important Alpenglow extensions are coming,” Watt stated. Alpenglow rolls out in two phases: first is Votor, its voting protocol, which is already live on the platform; second is Rotor, a single relay layer planned for a later release that will replace Turbine, the protocol that spreads a block’s data across the network.

Third is Performance, where network compute capacity doubles and transactions use 80% fewer compute units for token accounts. Last is Expressivity, which involves vector processing for models running fully onchain and an increase from 64 to 96 accounts per transaction.

According to recent reports, watt also spoke about improvements in onchain development: “The cost of storing data on Solana came down by 27% this year. And just in the coming two weeks, we're going to bring this thing down by another 7x.”.
